How cold storage is changing produce logistics in Nashik

By Meera Kulkarni, Farm Ledger correspondent

Ten years ago a tomato grown near Nashik had about two days to reach a buyer before it began to soften. Traders loaded open trucks before dawn, drove to the Vashi market in Navi Mumbai, and sold whatever arrived in saleable condition. Cold storage has changed that arithmetic for the growers who can reach it, and the change is visible in the prices they now negotiate.

Three pre-cooling and storage units opened in the district between 2019 and 2023. Each holds between 200 and 500 tonnes at temperatures between 8 and 12 degrees Celsius, which is enough to extend the shelf life of tomatoes by roughly a week and of grapes by several weeks. Operators charge by the crate per day, and most growers rent space only for the days a market glut would otherwise force a distress sale.

What buyers now ask for

Institutional buyers such as supermarket chains and hotel suppliers have started to specify the temperature at which produce must be held between the farm gate and the loading dock. Several growers told us that a temperature log, printed or sent as a message, is now part of the paperwork that accompanies each lot, much like the weighbridge slip.

CropTypical shelf life without coolingWith cold storage
Tomato3 to 4 days10 to 12 days
Grapes5 days3 to 4 weeks

The economics still favour larger growers. A smallholder with two acres rarely produces enough in one picking to fill a pallet, and sharing a crate with a neighbour requires trust and coordination that no app has solved yet. Cooperative societies that aggregate lots before they reach the unit report the best results, because the aggregation fee is smaller than the price premium a cold chain earns.
